description: This is our first hackathon, hoping to build innovative models. We are computer scientists with a background in NLP and RAG.
summary:
Fire is one of the most serious dangers a crew in space can face. Apollo 1, Apollo 13, Mir and Artemis II all showed how fast a fire or an alarm can become a crisis. NASA's next homes, a Moon base and pressurized rovers, will hold more oxygen than Earth's air, so materials there will burn more easily. NASA has studied flames in orbit for years, but the results are spread across many investigations and hard to interpret.

Flame in Freefall brings that research together in one AI-powered dashboard. Engineers, researchers and students can see what each experiment tested and compare experiments side by side. They can follow the evidence for preventing, detecting and suppressing fires, and find the studies that matter for a spacecraft, a lunar base or Mars. They can also pull data for their own models. Freefall AI answers questions in plain language and cites its sources.

Every insight is traceable: charts are computed directly from NASA's measured tests, and rankings explain each score. Predictive fire scenarios let users test conditions against real experiments, and the dashboard connects space research to fire safety on Earth, from water-mist extinguishers to firefighter gear.
details:
What it does

Flame in Freefall is an AI-powered dashboard that turns NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) combustion research into clear fire-safety answers for spacecraft, space stations, lunar and Martian bases, and pressurized rovers.

  • 🔥 Interactive story: a scroll-driven introduction shows how gravity reshapes a flame and why fire in space is so dangerous.
  • 🔎 Investigations: every PSI combustion study in one place, showing objectives, fuels, test conditions, variables and sensors, with side-by-side comparison.
  • 🛡️ Fire-safety insights: measured evidence for prevention, detection and suppression, with findings that explain why each matters for next-generation equipment.
  • 🚀 Mission relevance: studies ranked for the ISS, a Moon base, rovers, Mars or a spacesuit, with every score explained.
  • 📊 Data for modeling: load NASA's cleaned tables or upload your own data.
  • 🧪 Fire scenarios: model predictions checked against the nearest real experiments.
  • 🤖 Freefall AI: answers questions in plain language from NASA data, documents and combustion calculators, and cites every source.

Highlights

  • ✅ Every insight is traceable: charts are computed directly from NASA's measured tests, and every answer links back to PSI.
  • 🌙 Bounding the Moon and Mars: with no partial-gravity data yet, we frame lunar and Martian conditions between microgravity and Earth-gravity results.
  • 🧠 AI that shows its work: Freefall AI combines data queries, document search and scientific calculators, and checks its own numbers.
  • 📈 Honest models: predictions appear only when a model proves more reliable than a simple baseline.
  • 🌍 Back on Earth: links space research to water-mist extinguishers, smoke detection and firefighter gear.

How it works

Python converters clean NASA's PSI tables, which come in many formats, into one consistent dataset with a source for every record. A FastAPI backend computes the evidence, rankings and model predictions. A LangGraph AI agent combines data tools, a research library and combustion calculators to give cited answers. A Next.js frontend brings it together with interactive charts and 3D animation.

Tools

Area

Tools

Frontend

Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS

Visualization

Plotly.js, Three.js, GSAP

Backend & ML

Python, FastAPI, pandas, scikit-learn

AI

LangGraph, LangChain, LiteLLM, an OpenAI model, a retrieval index

Data

NASA PSI, NASA fact sheets, NIST fire-science publications

Impact

Flame in Freefall helps engineers, researchers and students turn years of orbital experiments into decisions: which materials to screen, how detectors should work, and which suppressants to use. It also shows where future tests, such as those at lunar gravity, will add the most value, making the next giant leap a safer one.

Factors we considered

Scientific honesty (findings stated exactly as measured, with limits shown), data quality (cleaned tables, tracked sources), audience (from students to experts), accessibility (color-blind-safe charts, plain language) and scope (habitable environments, as the challenge asks).
